title: Exponential Growth and Decay
lead: A quantity whose rate of change is proportional to its size follows $y=y_{0}e^{kt}:$ exponential growth when k is positive, with a constant doubling time, as for bacteria and continuously compounded interest; exponential decay when the exponent is negative, with a constant half-life, as for radiocarbon. Newton’s law of cooling becomes exponential decay after a change of variables.
objectives: Use the exponential growth model in applications, including population growth and compound interest.
Explain the concept of doubling time.
Use the exponential decay model in applications, including radioactive decay and Newton’s law of cooling.
summary_html:
• Exponential growth and exponential decay are two of the most common applications of exponential functions.
  • Systems that exhibit exponential growth follow a model of the form $y=y_{0}e^{kt}.$
  • In exponential growth, the rate of growth is proportional to the quantity present. In other words, $\kyprime=ky.$
  • Systems that exhibit exponential growth have a constant doubling time, which is given by $(\ln2)/k.$
  • Systems that exhibit exponential decay follow a model of the form $y=y_{0}e^{-kt}.$
  • Systems that exhibit exponential decay have a constant half-life, which is given by $(\ln2)/k.$

exercises.prompt: Consider a population of bacteria that grows according to the function $f(t)=500e^{0.05t},$ where $t$ is measured in minutes. How many bacteria are present in the population after 4 hours? When does the population reach $100$ million bacteria?

parts.hint: Use the process from the previous example.

answer.solution: There are $81,377,396$ bacteria in the population after $4$ hours. The population reaches $100$ million bacteria after $244.12$ minutes.

exercises.prompt: Suppose the room is warmer $(75\text{°}\text{F})$ and, after $2$ minutes, the coffee has cooled only to $185\text{°}\text{F}.$ When is the coffee first cool enough to serve? When is the coffee be too cold to serve? Round answers to the nearest half minute.

parts.hint: Use the process from the previous example.

answer.solution: The coffee is first cool enough to serve about $3.5$ minutes after it is poured. The coffee is too cold to serve about $7$ minutes after it is poured.

exercises.prompt: If we have $100$ g of $\text{carbon-}14,$ how much is left after $500$ years? If an artifact that originally contained $100$ g of carbon now contains $20g$ of carbon, how old is it? Round the answer to the nearest hundred years.

parts.hint: Use the process from the previous example.

answer.solution: A total of $94.13$ g of carbon remains. The artifact is approximately $13,300$ years old.

exercises.prompt:
True or False? If true, prove it. If false, find the true answer.

The doubling time for $y=e^{ct}$ is $(\ln(2))/(\ln(c)).$

answer.solution: False. $e^{cT}=2$ gives $cT=\ln 2,$ so the doubling time of $y=e^{ct}$ is $T=\frac{\ln 2}{c},$ not $\frac{\ln 2}{\ln c}.$ (The formula $\frac{\ln 2}{\ln c}$ is the doubling time of $y=c^{t}.$)

exercises.prompt:
True or False? If true, prove it. If false, find the true answer.

If you invest $\text{＄}500,$ an annual rate of interest of $3\text{\%}$ yields more money in the first year than a $2.5\text{\%}$ continuous rate of interest.

True or False? If true, prove it. If false, find the true answer.

If you leave a $100\text{°}\text{C}$ pot of tea at room temperature $(25\text{°}\text{C})$ and an identical pot in the refrigerator $(5\text{°}\text{C}),$ with $k=0.02,$ the tea in the refrigerator reaches a drinkable temperature $(70\text{°}\text{C})$ more than $5$ minutes before the tea at room temperature.

answer.solution: True. By Newton’s law of cooling, $T=(100-T_{a})e^{-0.02t}+T_{a}$ with t in minutes. At room temperature, $70=75e^{-0.02t}+25$ gives $e^{-0.02t}=0.6$ and $t=\frac{\ln(5/3)}{0.02}\approx 25.5$ minutes. In the refrigerator, $70=95e^{-0.02t}+5$ gives $e^{-0.02t}=\frac{13}{19}$ and $t=\frac{\ln(19/13)}{0.02}\approx 19.0$ minutes. The refrigerated tea is drinkable about 6.6 minutes sooner.

True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

If the half-life of $\text{seaborgium-}266$ is $360$ ms, then $k=(\ln(2))/360.$

answer.solution: True, for the decay model $y=y_{0}e^{-kt}$ with t in milliseconds: the half-life is $(\ln 2)/k,$ so $360=(\ln 2)/k$ and $k=(\ln 2)/360\approx 0.00193$ per millisecond. Written as $y=y_{0}e^{kt},$ the constant would be negative, $k=-(\ln 2)/360.$

It is noon and $45\text{°}\text{F}$ outside and the temperature of the body is $78\text{°}\text{F}.$ You know the cooling constant is $k=0.00824\text{°}\text{F/min}.$ When did the victim die, assuming that a human’s temperature is $98\text{°}\text{F}$ ?

[T] The best-fit exponential curve to these data is given by $y=40.71+{1.224}^{x}.$ Why do you think the gains of the market were unsustainable? Use first and second derivatives to help justify your answer. What would this model predict the Dow Jones industrial average to be in $2014$ ?

answer.solution: With $y=40.71+1.224^{x},$ $x$ years after 1920, $y'=1.224^{x}\ln 1.224>0$ and $y''=1.224^{x}(\ln 1.224)^{2}>0:$ the average rises, and the rise itself grows in proportion to $1.224^{x},$ about $22\%$ more each year. Gains that compound like this demand ever larger buying to keep up, which cannot last. For 2014, $x=94,$ and the model predicts $y=40.71+1.224^{94}\approx 178{,}000{,}000,$ about 178 million, far beyond any value the average has reached.

footnotes.html: The key adds $k=\frac{\ln(2)}{t};$ that is the constant of the decay model written $y=e^{-kt}.$ For $y=e^{kt}$ as the exercise writes it, $k=\frac{\ln(1/2)}{t}=-\frac{\ln(2)}{t},$ which is why the statement is true.
